journey_description: Comprehensive step-by-step roadmap for U.S. citizens petitioning for their parent (IR-5) via consular processing.

chapters.chapter_description: File Form I-130 with USCIS to begin the IR-5 parent visa process for your parent.

steps.step_description: Check whether the petitioner and parent relationship qualify for an IR-5 immigrant visa petition
actions: Verify the petitioner is a U.S. citizen
Confirm the petitioner is at least 21 years old
Confirm core relationship evidence is available
Screen for possible immigrant visa inadmissibility issues
Plan for financial sponsorship and U.S. domicile

quest_data.title: Determine Eligibility
quest_data.subtitle: Before filing, confirm that the U.S. citizen petitioner, the parent-child relationship, and the parent beneficiary meet the core conditions for an IR-5 parent petition. Complete each section below.

quests.title: Petitioner is a U.S. citizen and at least 21
quests.subtitle: Confirm the petitioner is legally eligible to petition for a parent

screens.label: Petitioner Status
screens.question: What is the petitioner's current U.S. immigration or citizenship status?
screens.helper: Only a U.S. citizen may petition for a parent in the IR-5 category. A lawful permanent resident cannot petition for a parent.

options.label: U.S. citizen
Lawful Permanent Resident (green card holder)
options.sub: A green card holder cannot file an IR-5 petition for a parent.

options.label: Not sure
Other / none of these

screens.label: Petitioner Age
screens.question: Is the U.S. citizen petitioner at least 21 years old?
screens.helper: A U.S. citizen must be at least 21 years old to petition for a parent.

options.label: Yes, the petitioner is 21 or older
No, the petitioner is under 21
options.sub: The petition cannot be filed until the U.S. citizen petitioner reaches age 21.

options.label: Not sure

screens.label: How Citizenship Was Obtained
screens.question: How did the petitioner become a U.S. citizen?
screens.helper: Citizenship by birth, acquisition, derivation, or naturalization may qualify. Select the path that applies.

options.label: Born in the United States
Born abroad and acquired or derived U.S. citizenship
Naturalized as a U.S. citizen
Not sure

screens.label: Proof of Citizenship
screens.question: Does the petitioner have accepted proof of U.S. citizenship?
screens.helper: The petitioner generally needs one valid document proving U.S. citizenship.

items: U.S. birth certificate
Valid or previously issued U.S. passport
Certificate of Naturalization
Certificate of Citizenship
Consular Report of Birth Abroad

options.label: Yes, at least one accepted document is available
Not yet, but it can be obtained
No, and obtaining proof may be difficult
Not sure

screens.label: Identity Consistency
screens.question: Do the petitioner's citizenship and birth records consistently show the petitioner's name and date of birth?
screens.helper: Differences may be explainable, but legal name-change or discrepancy evidence should be prepared before filing.

options.label: Yes, the records are consistent
There is a difference, but legal supporting evidence is available
There is a difference and supporting evidence is not available yet
Not sure

Continue to the relationship section.' }; })()

quests.title: A qualifying parent-child relationship exists
quests.subtitle: Identify the legal relationship between the petitioner and the parent beneficiary

screens.label: Parent Relationship Type
screens.question: Which relationship best describes the parent beneficiary?
screens.helper: The evidence and legal requirements differ depending on whether the beneficiary is the petitioner's mother, father, stepparent, or adoptive parent.

options.label: Biological or legal mother
Biological father, parents were married before or at the petitioner's birth
Biological father, parents were not married at the petitioner's birth
Stepparent
Adoptive parent
Foster parent, guardian, relative, or person who raised the petitioner without a qualifying legal relationship
Not sure

screens.label: Birth Record
screens.question: Does the petitioner's birth certificate or equivalent civil birth record identify the parent beneficiary?
screens.helper: A birth record naming the parent is primary relationship evidence in many IR-5 cases, though additional evidence is required for some father, step-parent, and adoption scenarios.

options.label: Yes, the parent is correctly named
The parent is named, but there are spelling, date, or identity differences
No, the parent is not named
The birth record is unavailable
Not sure

screens.label: Relationship Authenticity
screens.question: Is the claimed parent-child relationship genuine and supported by truthful civil or family records?
screens.helper: USCIS requires a real qualifying relationship. False parentage, altered records, or material misrepresentation can cause denial and serious immigration consequences.

options.label: Yes, the relationship and records are genuine
There may be inaccurate or conflicting information in the records
No, the claimed relationship is not legally or factually genuine
Not sure

quests.result_logic: (function() { if (answers['q2s1'] === 'guardian_other' || answers['q2s3'] === 'no') return { state: 'stop', title: 'A qualifying legal parent relationship has not been established', body: 'A foster parent, guardian, extended relative, or person who raised the petitioner does not automatically qualify as a parent for an IR-5 petition. The relationship must satisfy the immigration-law definition of parent.' }; if (answers['q2s1'] === 'unsure' || answers['q2s2'] === 'no' || answers['q2s2'] === 'unavailable' || answers['q2s2'] === 'unsure' || answers['q2s3'] === 'conflict' || answers['q2s3'] === 'unsure') return { state: 'review', title: 'The parent-child relationship needs closer review', body: 'The relationship type or primary civil evidence is unclear, missing, or inconsistent. Secondary evidence may be possible, but the correct legal relationship category should be confirmed before filing.' }; if (answers['q2s2'] === 'mismatch') return { state: 'caution', title: 'The relationship appears plausible, record discrepancies need documentation', body: 'The birth record identifies the parent, but identity differences should be resolved with name-change records, corrected civil documents, older records, or other credible evidence.' }; return { state: 'pass', title: 'A qualifying parent relationship appears to exist', body: 'The selected relationship appears potentially eligible and primary relationship evidence is identifiable. Complete the relationship-specific section next.' }; })()

quests.title: Relationship-specific requirements are satisfied
quests.subtitle: Check the special legal rules that may apply to a father, stepparent, or adoptive parent

screens.label: Parents' Marriage
screens.question: If the beneficiary is the petitioner's father, were the petitioner's parents legally married before the petitioner was born or while the petitioner was still legally eligible for legitimation?
screens.helper: For some father petitions, the parents' marriage and the law governing legitimation affect what evidence is required. Select not applicable for a mother, stepparent, or adoptive-parent case.

options.label: Yes, the parents were legally married
No, the parents were not legally married
Not applicable, this is not a biological-father case
Not sure

screens.label: Father-Child Relationship
screens.question: If the petitioner's parents were not married, was there a genuine father-child relationship before the petitioner turned 21 or married, whichever occurred first?
screens.helper: Evidence may include financial support, living together, regular contact, school or medical involvement, recognition of the child, correspondence, or other proof of an active parental relationship.

options.label: Yes, a genuine father-child relationship existed during the required period
No, there was no meaningful father-child relationship during that period
Not applicable, parents were married or this is not a biological-father case
Not sure

screens.label: Stepparent Formation
screens.question: If filing for a stepparent, did the stepparent marry the petitioner's biological or legal parent before the petitioner turned 18?
screens.helper: The marriage creating the step-relationship must generally have occurred before the petitioner's 18th birthday.

options.label: Yes, the marriage occurred before the petitioner turned 18
No, the marriage occurred on or after the petitioner's 18th birthday
Not applicable, this is not a stepparent case
Not sure

screens.label: Step-Relationship Continuity
screens.question: If filing for a stepparent, is the marriage that created the step-relationship still legally valid, or did it end only after the qualifying relationship was established?
screens.helper: Divorce, death, and later family events can affect whether a step-relationship continues to qualify. Complex cases should be reviewed individually.

options.label: Yes, the qualifying marriage remains valid
The marriage ended by death or divorce
Not applicable, this is not a stepparent case
Not sure

screens.label: Adoption Timing
screens.question: If filing for an adoptive parent, was the adoption completed before the petitioner turned 16, or before 18 under the qualifying sibling exception?
screens.helper: Family-based adoption rules are technical. An adoption completed after the applicable age limit generally does not create the required immigration relationship.

options.label: Yes, adoption met the applicable age rule
No, adoption occurred after the applicable age limit
Not applicable, this is not an adoptive-parent case
Not sure

screens.label: Adoptive Custody and Residence
screens.question: If filing for an adoptive parent, did the petitioner have at least two years of legal custody and two years of joint residence with the adoptive parent?
screens.helper: The two-year legal-custody and joint-residence requirements may be accumulated before or after adoption, but the evidence and legal rules should be reviewed carefully.

options.label: Yes, both two-year requirements are satisfied
No, one or both requirements are not satisfied
Not applicable, this is not an adoptive-parent case
Not sure

quests.result_logic: (function() { const type = answers['q2s1']; if (type === 'stepparent' && answers['q3s3'] === 'no') return { state: 'stop', title: 'The step-relationship was created too late for IR-5 eligibility', body: 'For a stepparent to qualify as a parent, the marriage creating the step-relationship generally must have occurred before the petitioner turned 18.' }; if (type === 'adoptive' && (answers['q3s5'] === 'no' || answers['q3s6'] === 'no')) return { state: 'stop', title: 'The adoption requirements do not appear to be satisfied', body: 'An adoptive-parent petition generally requires compliance with the applicable adoption-age rule plus two years of legal custody and two years of joint residence. This case should not proceed as a standard IR-5 filing without legal review.' }; if (type === 'father_unmarried' && (answers['q3s2'] === 'no' || answers['q3s2'] === 'unsure')) return { state: 'review', title: 'The biological-father relationship requires legal and evidentiary review', body: 'Where the parents were not married, eligibility may depend on legitimation law or proof of a genuine father-child relationship before the petitioner turned 21 or married. Gather contemporaneous evidence and obtain legal review if the relationship history is unclear.' }; if (answers['q3s1'] === 'unsure' || answers['q3s3'] === 'unsure' || answers['q3s4'] === 'ended' || answers['q3s4'] === 'unsure' || answers['q3s5'] === 'unsure' || answers['q3s6'] === 'unsure') return { state: 'review', title: 'A relationship-specific rule needs clarification', body: 'The selected parent category involves a timing, marriage, custody, residence, or relationship-continuity issue that should be resolved before filing.' }; return { state: 'pass', title: 'Relationship-specific eligibility appears on track', body: 'No disqualifying issue was identified under the relationship-specific rules selected in this assessment.' }; })()

quests.title: Core relationship evidence can be documented
quests.subtitle: Confirm that the petitioner can prove both identity and the qualifying parent-child relationship

screens.label: Primary Relationship Documents
screens.question: Which primary relationship records are currently available?
screens.helper: Select all that apply. The exact required combination depends on the relationship category.

options.label: Petitioner's birth certificate naming the parent
Parents' marriage certificate
Parent beneficiary's identity and civil records
Stepparent marriage certificate
Final adoption decree
Legal-custody and joint-residence evidence
None of these are currently available

screens.label: Secondary Evidence
screens.question: If a primary record is unavailable or inconsistent, is credible secondary evidence available?
screens.helper: Secondary evidence may help when a civil record is genuinely unavailable, late-registered, or inconsistent. USCIS may also request additional evidence or DNA testing in appropriate cases.

options.label: Family Registration Certificate or equivalent family record
School, medical, vaccination, or religious records created earlier in life
Old identity documents, passports, or household records
Financial support, correspondence, photographs, or co-residence evidence
Affidavits from persons with personal knowledge
Official record-unavailability letter
Not needed, complete primary evidence is available
No secondary evidence is available

screens.label: Translations
screens.question: Are complete English translations available for documents that are not in English?
screens.helper: Any foreign-language document submitted to USCIS must include a full English translation with the translator's certification of competence and accuracy.

options.label: Yes, translations are complete and certified
Not yet, translations can be prepared
No, translation arrangements are unclear
Not applicable, all records are in English

Do not file until the relationship-document strategy has been reviewed and the required records have been obtained or their unavailability properly documented.' }; if (p.includes('none') || s.includes('none') || answers['q4s3'] === 'can_get' || answers['q4s3'] === 'no') return { state: 'caution', title: 'The relationship may qualify, evidence preparation is incomplete', body: 'Some required civil records, secondary evidence, or translations still need to be gathered. Address these gaps before filing to reduce the risk of rejection, request for evidence, or denial.' }; return { state: 'pass', title: 'The relationship appears documentable', body: 'Primary records or credible backup evidence are identifiable, and translation needs appear manageable.' }; })()

quests.title: Additional IR-5 planning and visa ineligibility screening
quests.subtitle: Screen for common admissibility, sponsorship, domicile, and case-structure concerns

screens.label: Parent's Immigration History
screens.question: Has the parent beneficiary ever been refused a U.S. visa, denied an immigration benefit, removed, deported, ordered to leave, or accused of fraud or misrepresentation?
screens.helper: A prior refusal does not automatically prevent approval, but fraud, removal, or misrepresentation may create serious legal issues.

options.label: No, none of these apply
Yes, at least one applies
Not sure

screens.label: Criminal History
screens.question: Has the parent beneficiary ever been arrested, charged, convicted, cautioned, or involved in a criminal case anywhere in the world?
screens.helper: Even old, dismissed, or minor cases may need to be disclosed and documented.

options.label: No, no criminal history
Yes, at least one incident exists
Not sure

screens.label: Prior U.S. Presence
screens.question: Has the parent beneficiary ever entered without inspection, overstayed, worked without authorization, accumulated unlawful presence, or violated U.S. immigration status?
screens.helper: Some violations may trigger inadmissibility bars, especially after departure from the United States.

options.label: No, none of these apply
Yes, at least one applies
Not sure

screens.label: Health and Vaccination
screens.question: Is there a known medical, communicable-disease, substance-related, or vaccination issue that may arise during the immigrant visa medical examination?
screens.helper: The panel physician makes the medical determination. A health condition does not automatically mean the parent is ineligible.

options.label: No known issue
Yes, a medical or vaccination concern may arise
Not sure

screens.label: Public Charge and Financial Sponsorship
screens.question: Can the petitioner likely submit Form I-864 and meet the financial sponsorship requirement through income, qualifying assets, household-member income, or a joint sponsor?
screens.helper: The petitioner must submit Form I-864 even when a joint sponsor is used. Financial sponsorship is primarily handled at the NVC stage, but planning should begin now.

options.label: Yes, sponsorship appears manageable
Possibly, a joint sponsor or assets may be needed
No, no viable sponsorship plan is currently available
Not sure

screens.label: U.S. Domicile
screens.question: Does the petitioner maintain a U.S. domicile, or can the petitioner show a concrete plan to re-establish U.S. domicile no later than the parent's admission?
screens.helper: A petitioner living abroad may still qualify to file Form I-130, but must satisfy the U.S. domicile requirement for Form I-864 before visa issuance.

options.label: Yes, U.S. domicile is established
Petitioner lives abroad but has a documented plan to re-establish domicile
No, there is currently no U.S. domicile plan
Not sure

screens.label: Separate Petition for Each Parent
screens.question: If both parents will immigrate, is the petitioner prepared to file a separate Form I-130 for each parent?
screens.helper: IR-5 petitions do not provide derivative status. A spouse or other child of the parent cannot immigrate through the same parent petition.

options.label: Yes, only one parent is immigrating or separate petitions will be filed
No, we expected both parents or other relatives to use one petition
Not sure

steps.notes: The petitioner must be a U.S. citizen aged 21 or older. The beneficiary must qualify as the petitioner's parent under U.S. immigration law. Each parent requires a separate Form I-130 and IR-5 case.

risk_signals.disclaimer: Educational screening based on USCIS and Department of State requirements. It is not an official USCIS or consular eligibility determination and is not legal advice.

patterns.title: Petitioner is not a U.S. citizen
patterns.advisory: Only a U.S. citizen may petition for a parent. A lawful permanent resident cannot file an IR-5 parent petition.

patterns.title: Petitioner is under 21
patterns.advisory: A U.S. citizen must be at least 21 years old to petition for a parent. Filing must wait until the petitioner reaches age 21.

patterns.title: Birth record is missing or inconsistent
patterns.advisory: Obtain the correct civil birth record if available. If unavailable or inconsistent, prepare record-unavailability evidence, secondary contemporaneous records, identity evidence, and a clear discrepancy explanation.
patterns.source_basis: Form I-130 Instructions; USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 6, Part B

patterns.title: Biological-father case involving birth outside marriage
patterns.advisory: Review legitimation law and gather evidence of a bona fide father-child relationship before the petitioner turned 21 or married, as applicable. These cases require relationship-specific evidence.
patterns.source_basis: INA 101(b)(1); Form I-130 Instructions; USCIS Policy Manual

patterns.title: Step-relationship created after age 18
patterns.advisory: A marriage creating a step-parent relationship generally must occur before the child turns 18. A relationship created later does not normally qualify for IR-5.

patterns.title: Adoption age, custody, or residence requirements are not established
patterns.advisory: Adoptive-parent petitions generally require adoption before age 16, or age 18 under the sibling exception, plus two years of legal custody and two years of joint residence. Obtain specialist legal review before filing if any element is uncertain.

patterns.title: Beneficiary is only a guardian, foster parent, or caregiver
patterns.advisory: Guardianship, foster care, financial support, or raising a child does not by itself create a qualifying parent relationship under the IR-5 category.

patterns.title: Multiple parents expected to use one petition
patterns.advisory: File a separate Form I-130 for each parent. IR-5 beneficiaries do not receive derivative status for a spouse or other relatives.
patterns.source_basis: Form I-130 filing structure; immediate-relative classification rules

patterns.title: Parent has prior removal, fraud, or misrepresentation history
patterns.advisory: Obtain all prior decisions, visa records, removal documents, and immigration filings. Fraud or willful misrepresentation may create a permanent inadmissibility ground unless a waiver is legally available.

patterns.title: Parent has an arrest, charge, or conviction
patterns.advisory: Collect certified court and police records for every incident and obtain legal analysis before filing or consular processing.

patterns.title: Parent has unlawful-presence or immigration-status history
patterns.advisory: Departure after unlawful presence may trigger three-year, ten-year, or other inadmissibility bars. Review the complete entry, exit, and status history before choosing consular processing.

patterns.title: Financial sponsorship may be insufficient
patterns.advisory: The petitioner must submit Form I-864. If income is insufficient, review qualifying assets, household-member income, or a joint sponsor. A joint sponsor does not replace the petitioner's own I-864.
patterns.source_basis: INA 213A; Form I-864 Instructions; Department of State Affidavit of Support guidance

patterns.title: Petitioner may not satisfy U.S. domicile
patterns.advisory: A petitioner living abroad must establish an existing U.S. domicile or show concrete steps to re-establish domicile no later than the parent's admission as a permanent resident.
patterns.source_basis: INA 213A; Form I-864 Instructions; Department of State Affidavit of Support guidance

steps.step_description: Prepare the documents needed for the IR-5 parent petition. steps.pakistanSpecific: For Pakistani records, use documents issued by the competent local civil authority, such as the relevant Union Council, municipal authority, cantonment board, CDA where applicable, or NADRA-supported civil registration system. The petitioner's birth record is the central IR-5 relationship document. FRC, CRC/B-Form, school, medical, vaccination, and older identity records may support a case where the primary record is unavailable or inconsistent. A Pakistani guardianship order is not automatically equivalent to a qualifying adoption under U.S. immigration law.
stageWarnings: Do not mark the parent's Police Character Certificate as required for the USCIS I-130 filing.
Do not obtain time-sensitive police or medical documents unnecessarily early.
A separate Form I-130 and separate evidence packet are required for each parent.
The parent beneficiary does not receive derivative beneficiaries through the IR-5 petition.
Relationship documents differ materially for a mother, married father, unmarried father, stepparent, and adoptive parent.

steps.step_description: Decide between Online vs. Paper filing

filing_data.title: Decide Filing Method
filing_data.subtitle: Choose how to file Form I-130 with USCIS. Both methods are fully accepted and take the same amount of time to process, select the one that works best for you.

methods.title: ONLINE FILING
methods.name: File Online
methods.subtitle: via USCIS online account
features: Receive an electronic receipt number
Upload supporting documents digitally
Track and manage the case online
Saves $50 compared with paper filing

methods.title: PAPER FILING
methods.name: File by Mail
methods.subtitle: mail the petition packet to USCIS
features: Submit printed forms and document copies
Pay electronically by card or ACH using the required payment form
Receive Form I-797 receipt notice after acceptance
Same eligibility and adjudication standards as online filing

filing_data.footerNote: Fees as of May 2026 per the USCIS G-1055 fee schedule. Processing time is generally similar for both methods. A separate Form I-130 and separate filing fee are required for each parent. Always verify current fees and filing requirements at uscis.gov before filing.

screens.question: Is an attorney or accredited representative managing the filing for you?
screens.helper: If a representative is handling the paperwork, they typically decide the filing method, this walkthrough may not apply.

items: Attorneys can file I-130 online via their USCIS representative account, or by mailing a paper packet, both work
Ask your attorney or document preparer which method they prefer before deciding

options.label: Yes, a representative is handling this
No, I'm filing on my own
Not sure yet

screens.question: Can the petitioner create and manage a USCIS online account?
screens.helper: Online filing requires a free USCIS account at my.uscis.gov, used to complete the form, upload documents, and pay the filing fee.

items: Account setup takes a few minutes and just needs a valid email address
Your USCIS account also delivers notices, requests for evidence, and case updates
Paper filers can add their case to a USCIS account later using the mailed receipt number

options.label: Yes, comfortable setting up and using an online account
No, online accounts aren't practical right now
Not sure

screens.question: Are the required documents available in digital form for upload?
screens.helper: Online filing requires uploading scanned or photographed copies. Paper filing uses physical copies sent by mail.

items: PDF, JPG, or PNG are accepted, a phone camera usually works fine
Documents must be clear and fully legible
A flatbed scanner gives better results for dense documents like a Nikah Nama

options.label: Yes, documents are ready or easy to scan
No, physical copies only, hard to digitize right now
Not sure

screens.question: Does the petitioner have a preference for how to file?
screens.helper: Both methods are fully valid. Your comfort level is a legitimate deciding factor, there is no wrong choice.

options.label: Prefer online, convenient and saves $50
Prefer paper, more comfortable mailing a physical packet
No strong preference, happy with whatever works best

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Go to the official USCIS fee schedule page
guide_steps.text: Open the official USCIS fee schedule at uscis.gov/g-1055 and select I-130, Petition for Alien Relative from the form dropdown to see the current filing fees. This is the only place you should confirm the fee amount, do not rely on any saved screenshot or old amount.

guide_steps.title: Check the current I-130 filing fees
guide_steps.text: After selecting I-130, the page shows the current filing fees for Form I-130. Review the fee for Paper Filing before preparing your payment. Have the exact amount ready before assembling the final mailing packet.
guide_steps.note: You are filing by paper, so the applicable fee is the Paper Filing Fee. Prepare payment for this exact amount before packet assembly.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Choose your paper-filing payment method
guide_steps.text:
USCIS no longer accepts personal/business checks, money orders, or cashier's checks. You must use one of the approved payment or fee exemption options:
  • Option A: Pay by credit, debit, or prepaid card using Form G-1450 (Authorization for Credit Card Transactions).
  • Option B: Pay from a U.S. bank account (ACH) using Form G-1650.
  • Option C: If eligible for an exemption from the higher paper filing fee, submit Form G-1651 (Exemption for Paper Fee Payment).
USCIS Form G-1651 Exemption Requirements
To request an exemption, you must certify that electronic payment and collection methods are not possible and you meet 1 or more of the following requirements:
  • You do not have access to banking services or electronic payment systems;
  • Electronic disbursement would cause you undue hardship (infrastructure barriers in remote/foreign areas or personal limitations), as discussed in 31 C.F.R. Part 208 (GovInfo Official Citation ↗);
  • Non-electronic transactions are necessary or desirable for national security or law enforcement reasons; or
  • There are other circumstances as determined by the secretary of the treasury, as reflected in regulations or other guidance.
Hardship categories under 31 C.F.R. § 208.4: Infrastructure barriers (foreign/remote regions lacking U.S. digital banking) and personal barriers (financial, physical, or technical inability to manage online banking).
guide_steps.note: Download and print Form G-1450, Form G-1650, or Form G-1651 from uscis.gov and fill it out completely before placing it in the packet.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Place payment at the front of the packet
guide_steps.text: Once the payment item is ready, whether it is a completed Form G-1450 (card), Form G-1650 (ACH), or Form G-1651 (Fee Exemption), place it at the very front of the mailing packet. The payment or fee exemption form should be the first thing USCIS sees when they open the envelope.

guide_steps.label: Mailing guide · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Assemble Filing Packet
guide_steps.text: Organize the completed paper filing into one final mailing packet before shipment. Place the payment and completed forms at the front, then add supporting evidence and translations behind them in a clean review order. Once everything is stacked, flip through the full packet one more time to confirm nothing is missing and every page is readable before sealing it.
guide_steps.note: Order matters. Payment first, forms next, then supporting documents and translations at the back. A quick final flip-through takes one minute and prevents a missing document from causing a rejection.

guide_steps.label: Mailing guide · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Confirm the current USCIS filing address
guide_steps.text: Before mailing, verify the current USCIS filing address for your paper submission so the packet goes to the correct location.
guide_steps.note: Do not mail to an old address saved from a previous screenshot or conversation.

guide_steps.label: Mailing guide · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Choose a trackable mailing service
guide_steps.text: Select a mailing carrier and shipping service that includes tracking and delivery confirmation before sending the packet to USCIS.
guide_steps.note: Tracking and delivery confirmation help prove the packet was successfully delivered to USCIS. Keep the receipt, you may need it later.

guide_steps.label: Mailing guide · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Mail the packet and save the tracking details
guide_steps.text: As soon as the packet is mailed, save the carrier and tracking number in Rahvana.
guide_steps.note: Do not wait until later to record the tracking number. Save it the same day you mail the packet.

guide_steps.label: Mailing guide · Step 5
guide_steps.title: Watch for delivery, then wait for the USCIS receipt notice
guide_steps.text: Once the carrier shows delivered, keep the proof and then watch for USCIS acceptance and the receipt notice.
guide_steps.note: After delivery, the paper path rejoins the same receipt-notice and case-tracking flow used in the online branch.

steps.step_description: During USCIS review, USCIS may issue a notice requesting additional evidence or information before making a decision. Identify the notice type so Rahvana can guide your specific response.

tool_data.title: USCIS Notice Received
tool_data.subtitle: USCIS may ask for additional evidence or information before deciding your petition. Identify the notice type below so Rahvana can guide your response.

alert.heading: Do not ignore this notice
alert.body: Missing the response deadline can result in your petition being denied — including denial based on abandonment. USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period.

intro_card.heading: Receiving a USCIS notice is not the end of the road
intro_card.body: Most notices give you an opportunity to respond before a final decision is made. The key is to read the notice carefully, respond to exactly what USCIS asked for, and submit a complete response before the deadline.

notice_types.label: I-797 — Approval Notice
notice_types.description: USCIS has approved your I-130 petition and issued an I-797 approval notice. Save the original notice and prepare for the NVC stage.

notice_types.label: RFE — Request for Evidence
notice_types.description: USCIS needs additional evidence or information before it can decide your petition. This is the most common notice. Receiving an RFE does not mean your petition has been denied.

notice_types.label: RFI — Request for Additional Information
notice_types.description: USCIS is asking for clarifying information. Similar in nature to an RFE but typically more limited in scope.

notice_types.label: RFO — Request for Original Document
notice_types.description: USCIS is requesting an original document. You may have submitted a copy where an original is required.

notice_types.label: NOID — Notice of Intent to Deny
notice_types.description: USCIS is considering denying your petition and is giving you a chance to respond. This is more serious than an RFE. Consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

notice_types.label: Denial — I-130 Petition Denied
notice_types.description: USCIS has issued a denial of your I-130 petition. Review the denial notice carefully — it explains the reasons and your available options such as appeal or motion.

notice_types.label: Other USCIS notice or request
notice_types.description: USCIS may send other types of requests such as biometrics appointments or interview notices. Follow the specific instructions on your notice.

where_to_find.title: Where to find your notice

items.detail: Log in to my.uscis.gov and check your case notices and messages. USCIS recommends checking your online account first.
Notices may also be sent by mail to the petitioner's address on file. Keep your address updated with USCIS.

where_to_find.note: If your USCIS online account shows an RFE, an online response portal may be available. Do not mail a duplicate response if you submit online.

deadline_warning.heading: Check the deadline on your actual notice
deadline_warning.body: Do not assume you have a specific number of days. The deadline is printed on your RFE or NOID notice. USCIS states that the maximum response period is generally 12 weeks, but the notice controls the actual deadline for your case.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Evidence · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for Evidence on your I-130 parent petition. This does not mean your petition is denied — USCIS is giving you an opportunity to provide the evidence needed to decide your case.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFE
guide_data.subtitle: A Request for Evidence (RFE) means USCIS needs more information before deciding your parent petition. This is your opportunity to provide the evidence that closes the gap.

alert.heading: An RFE does not mean your petition was denied
alert.body: Receiving an RFE means USCIS is giving you a chance to provide additional evidence before making a final decision. Many parent petitions are approved after a successful RFE response.

warning_banner.text: Submit your complete RFE response before the deadline printed on your notice. Do not send documents in pieces — USCIS treats a partial response as a request for a decision on the existing record.

common_rfe_reasons.title: Common reasons USCIS issues an IR-5 parent I-130 RFE
common_rfe_reasons.subtitle: Read your RFE notice first to identify exactly what USCIS is requesting. The categories below describe common areas for parent petitions — your response should address your specific notice, not all of these.

categories.label: Proof of qualifying parent-child relationship
categories.description: USCIS may require stronger evidence establishing the legal parent-child relationship between the U.S. citizen petitioner and the parent beneficiary.
evidence_examples: Petitioner's official birth certificate naming the parent
Mother: Petitioner's birth certificate showing mother's name
Father (parents married): Birth certificate + parents' marriage certificate (Nikah Nama & NADRA MRC)
Father (unmarried/legitimated): Proof of legitimation before age 18, or evidence of ongoing bona fide parent-child financial/emotional relationship before age 21
Stepparent: Marriage certificate showing marriage to biological parent before petitioner turned 18
Adoptive parent: Certified adoption decree before age 16 + proof of 2 years legal custody and joint residence
NADRA Family Registration Certificate (FRC) by Birth
DNA relationship testing (only if explicitly requested or suggested by USCIS from an AABB-accredited lab)
categories.important_note: Do not automatically send all of these. Read exactly what your RFE requests and provide evidence relevant to that specific relationship type.

categories.label: Missing, incomplete, or secondary civil documentation
categories.description: USCIS may determine that submitted birth or marriage documentation is insufficient, late-registered, or missing required civil registration details.
evidence_examples: NADRA-issued computerized birth certificate
Union Council official birth certificate
Certified English translations with translator certification
Secondary evidence for late-registered birth (school records, matriculation certificates, hospital records)
Affidavits of birth from older relatives with personal knowledge of the birth
NADRA Family Registration Certificate (FRC)
categories.important_note: For Pakistani civil documents, USCIS frequently requests NADRA-issued certificates alongside certified English translations and secondary birth evidence if the primary birth was registered late.

categories.label: Petitioner citizenship or age verification
categories.description: USCIS may request additional proof that the petitioner is a U.S. citizen and was at least 21 years old at the time of filing.
evidence_examples: Unexpired U.S. passport (copy of all biographical pages)
Certificate of Naturalization or Certificate of Citizenship
U.S. Birth Certificate (if born in the United States)
Consular Report of Birth Abroad (CRBA)

categories.label: Inconsistencies across documents
categories.description: If names, parent names, or dates of birth differ across documents (such as passport, CNIC/NICOP, birth certificate, FRC, and Form I-130), USCIS may request clarification.
evidence_examples: Explanation letter addressing specific discrepancies
One and the same affidavit explaining name spelling variations
Certified civil or NADRA correction records
Official legal name change documentation
categories.important_note: Name spelling variations and date discrepancies across Pakistani identity documents (CNIC, passport, Nikah Nama, FRC) are common. Address each discrepancy directly and specifically.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Don't panic — read your RFE first
guide_steps.text: An RFE does not mean your petition is denied. USCIS is asking for additional evidence before making a decision. Your first task is to obtain the actual RFE notice and read it carefully — every word of it.
guide_steps.note: Get the notice from your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or from physical mail. The online account is the recommended first place to check.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Identify exactly what USCIS is requesting
guide_steps.text: Do not randomly gather documents. The RFE will specifically identify what is deficient and what USCIS needs. Your response must directly address the specific issue identified in the RFE — nothing more, nothing less.
guide_steps.note: For example: 'Submit evidence demonstrating the parent-child relationship between petitioner and beneficiary' is different from 'Submit a certified English translation of the birth certificate.' Each requires a different response.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Check the deadline printed on your notice
guide_steps.text: The response deadline is printed on your RFE notice. Do not assume you have a specific number of days — the actual notice controls your deadline. USCIS policy states that extensions beyond the permitted response period are generally not granted.
guide_steps.note: Mark the deadline in your calendar immediately. Build in time to organize, review, and submit your response well before the deadline.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Organize your evidence by RFE request
guide_steps.text: Structure your evidence to match each item USCIS requested. Group documents under the specific request they address. For example — USCIS Request: Proof of parent-child relationship: Exhibit A — Petitioner NADRA birth certificate, Exhibit B — Parents' Nikah Nama & MRC, Exhibit C — Family Registration Certificate (FRC), Exhibit D — Secondary school records. This structure makes it easy for the USCIS officer to match your response to their request.
guide_steps.note: Clear organization significantly helps the reviewing officer understand your response and reduces the chance of important evidence being overlooked.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 5
guide_steps.title: Write a cover letter
guide_steps.text: Prepare a brief cover letter that explains: (1) what USCIS requested, (2) how your response addresses each specific request, and (3) what evidence is included and how it is organized. The cover letter is the roadmap for your response package.
guide_steps.note: The cover letter does not need to be lengthy. It should clearly summarize the response contents and make it easy for the officer to navigate your package.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 6
guide_steps.title: Assemble one complete response package
guide_steps.text: Gather your cover letter and all evidence together into one complete response package before submitting. USCIS policy states that when responding to an RFE, materials should generally be submitted together. A partial response is treated as a request for a decision on the record — USCIS does not wait for additional packages or issue another RFE.
guide_steps.note: Double-check that every document is included, every translation is certified, and the cover letter is accurate before you submit.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 7
guide_steps.title: Choose the correct submission method
guide_steps.text: Check whether your USCIS online account provides an RFE response portal for your case. If it does, follow the online submission instructions. If your case requires a mailed response, use the address and instructions specified in your RFE notice.
guide_steps.note: USCIS has specifically stated that users who respond online should NOT also mail a duplicate response. Follow the method indicated on your notice or in your USCIS account.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 8
guide_steps.title: Keep a complete copy of everything you submit
guide_steps.text: Before submitting, make copies of your complete response package, including the cover letter and all evidence. If submitting by mail, use a trackable carrier and save the tracking number. If submitting online, save a copy of the confirmation.
guide_steps.note: Your copy of the response is important if questions arise later about what was submitted and when.

citations.text: USCIS Policy Manual - Request For Evidence

after_submission.heading: After you submit your RFE response
after_submission.body: Your case returns to USCIS review. USCIS will consider the submitted evidence and issue one of these outcomes.

outcomes.label: Approval
outcomes.description: USCIS approves the I-130 petition. For consular processing, the case moves toward the National Visa Center (NVC) stage.

outcomes.label: Denial
outcomes.description: If the response does not establish eligibility, USCIS may deny the petition. The denial notice will explain available appeal and motion options.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If your RFE involves complex legal issues or you are uncertain how to respond, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Additional Information · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for Additional Information (RFI) on your I-130 petition. An RFI typically requests clarifying information and is generally narrower in scope than an RFE.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFI
guide_data.subtitle: A Request for Additional Information (RFI) means USCIS needs specific clarifying information before proceeding. Read the notice carefully and respond directly to what is asked.

alert.heading: An RFI does not mean your petition was denied
alert.body: USCIS is requesting clarifying information to continue processing your petition. Respond to exactly what is asked, before the deadline printed on the notice.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the RFI notice
guide_steps.text: Check your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or your physical mail for the RFI notice. Read the notice carefully to understand exactly what information USCIS is requesting.
guide_steps.note: An RFI is typically narrower in scope than an RFE. USCIS is asking for specific clarifying information, not a broad set of evidence.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFI notice. Note it immediately and plan your response with enough time to review everything before submitting.
guide_steps.note: USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period. Missing the deadline can result in a denial.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Prepare a clear, direct response
guide_steps.text: Respond directly to the information USCIS requested. Provide only what is asked — clear, focused, and accurate. Include a brief cover letter that identifies what was requested and how your response addresses it.
guide_steps.note: Clarity is key. A focused response that directly answers the question is more effective than a large unorganized package.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit one complete response
guide_steps.text: Assemble your complete response into a single submission. Do not submit in pieces. Use the submission method specified in your RFI notice — online portal if available in your USCIS account, or mail if instructed.
guide_steps.note: If submitting online, do not also mail a duplicate response. Keep a copy of everything you submit.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you are uncertain about your RFI response, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Original Document · Locate & submit original
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for an Original (RFO) document. USCIS is requesting that you submit the original version of a document you may have previously submitted as a copy.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFO
guide_data.subtitle: USCIS is requesting an original document. Identify the specific document requested, locate the original, and submit it following the instructions on your notice.

alert.heading: USCIS is asking for an original, not a copy
alert.body: Carefully read your RFO notice to identify exactly which document is required in original form. Submitting another copy will not satisfy the request.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Identify the specific document requested
guide_steps.text: Read your RFO notice carefully. USCIS will identify the specific document it is requesting in original form. Common examples include original birth certificates, original marriage certificates/Nikah Namas, or other original civil documents.
guide_steps.note: If you are unsure whether your document is truly the original versus a certified copy, contact the issuing authority to clarify.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFO notice. Mark it immediately. Plan enough time to locate the document, make a copy for your records, and prepare your submission.
guide_steps.note: Do not wait until close to the deadline. Locating original documents, especially civil documents from Pakistan, may take time.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Make a copy before submitting the original
guide_steps.text: Before sending any original document to USCIS, make a clear copy for your own records. USCIS receives many documents and originals are not always returned promptly, or may take significant time to be returned.
guide_steps.note: Keep your copy in a safe place. If the original is irreplaceable, consider consulting an immigration attorney about the best approach.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit using a secure, trackable method
guide_steps.text: Send the original document using a secure and trackable shipping method. Include a cover letter identifying the case receipt number, the RFO reference, and what document is enclosed. Follow the submission instructions in your RFO notice.
guide_steps.note: Keep the tracking number and delivery confirmation. Once the carrier shows delivered, save that proof.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you have concerns about submitting irreplaceable original documents, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Notice of Intent to Deny · Respond carefully before deadline
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) on your I-130 petition. A NOID is more serious than an RFE — USCIS is indicating it is considering denying your petition based on the current record and is giving you one opportunity to respond.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS NOID
guide_data.subtitle: A Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) means USCIS is considering denying your petition. This is your opportunity to respond with evidence and legal arguments before a final decision is made.

alert.heading: A NOID is more serious than an RFE
alert.body: USCIS is not simply asking for more evidence. It is indicating that based on the current record, it intends to deny your petition — and is giving you one opportunity to respond. Carefully review the reasons USCIS has stated. Because the response may require legal analysis, strongly consider getting help from a qualified immigration attorney.

noid_vs_rfe.title: NOID vs. RFE — the key difference

rfe.label: RFE
rfe.description: We need more evidence before we can make a decision.

noid.label: NOID
noid.description: Based on what we currently have, we are considering denying your petition. Here is why. You have one opportunity to respond.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the NOID notice immediately
guide_steps.text: Obtain the NOID notice from your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or from physical mail. Read the entire notice carefully. USCIS is required to identify the intended reasons for denial, explain deficiencies, and identify potentially missing evidence.
guide_steps.note: Understanding exactly what USCIS says is wrong is the foundation of your response. Do not skip or skim any part of the notice.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline immediately
guide_steps.text: The response deadline is printed on your NOID notice. Note it immediately and treat it as your hard deadline. Extensions are generally not granted.
guide_steps.note: Given the seriousness of a NOID, you should begin working on your response immediately — do not wait until close to the deadline.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Because a NOID response may require legal analysis and argumentation — not just evidence submission — strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney before preparing your response. An attorney can assess the specific deficiencies USCIS identified and advise on the best response strategy.
guide_steps.note: This is Rahvana's strongest recommendation for NOID situations. The consequences of a denial are significant — the response deserves careful legal attention.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Address each stated reason for the proposed denial
guide_steps.text: Your response must directly address each reason USCIS stated in the NOID. For each issue identified, explain why that reason does not support denial and provide evidence that counters or clarifies the issue.
guide_steps.note: A NOID response is not just an evidence package — it should include a legal argument explaining why, based on the law and facts, the petition should be approved.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 5
guide_steps.title: Submit one complete response before the deadline
guide_steps.text: Assemble your complete response — cover letter, legal arguments, and all supporting evidence — into a single submission. Follow the submission instructions on your NOID notice. Do not send documents in pieces.
guide_steps.note: Keep a complete copy of everything you submit, with proof of submission (tracking number or online confirmation).

guide_data.title: I-130 Denied — Review Your Options
guide_data.subtitle: An I-130 denial is a serious outcome, but it may not be the end of the road. Review the denial notice carefully and understand what options may be available.

alert.heading: Carefully review the denial notice
alert.body: The denial notice explains USCIS's specific reasons for the denial and states what appeal or motion options are available in your case. The correct next step depends entirely on the specific reasons for the denial and the facts of your case. Do not file an appeal or motion without understanding the denial first.

denial_options.title: Possible options after an I-130 denial
denial_options.subtitle: Which option is appropriate depends on the specific reasons for the denial and the circumstances of your case. The denial notice itself explains what options are available.

options.label: Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
options.description: Certain I-130 decisions can be appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals using Form EOIR-29 (Notice of Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals from a Decision of a DHS Officer). USCIS confirms that I-130 appeals are among the appeals filed using Form EOIR-29.
options.important: Appeals have strict deadlines. Check your denial notice for the deadline and the specific appeal procedure that applies to your case.

options.label: Motion to Reopen
options.description: A motion to reopen asks USCIS to reopen the case based on new facts or evidence that was not available at the time of the decision.
options.important: A motion to reopen is appropriate when there is new factual evidence that was not part of the original record. Review the denial carefully before pursuing this option.

options.label: Motion to Reconsider
options.description: A motion to reconsider asks USCIS to reconsider its decision based on an error of law or incorrect application of policy to the existing facts.
options.important: A motion to reconsider is appropriate when you believe USCIS made a legal error in the denial, not when you simply have new evidence.

options.label: File a new petition
options.description: Depending on the denial reason, it may sometimes be appropriate to file a new I-130 petition with corrected information or additional evidence. This should be carefully evaluated based on the specific denial reason.
options.important: Filing a new petition when an appeal or motion is more appropriate may not be the best strategy. Consult an immigration attorney.

attorney_recommendation.heading: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
attorney_recommendation.body: Determining the right strategy after an I-130 denial — appeal vs. motion vs. new petition — requires careful analysis of the denial reasons, the evidence record, and the applicable law. The wrong choice can waste time, resources, or foreclose other options. An experienced immigration attorney can help you evaluate the best path forward.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Read the denial notice completely
guide_steps.text: The denial notice contains the specific reasons USCIS denied the petition and explains what appeal or motion rights are available. Read it completely before deciding on any next step.
guide_steps.note: The denial notice is the most important document at this stage. Every option you consider must be evaluated against the specific reasons stated in the notice.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Note any deadlines for appeal or motion
guide_steps.text: If the denial notice indicates appeal or motion rights, it will also state the deadlines for filing. These deadlines are strict — missing them can eliminate certain options.
guide_steps.note: Do not delay in reviewing the notice and understanding the available deadlines. Begin consulting an attorney as soon as possible if you are considering an appeal or motion.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Consult a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Given the complexity of determining the right post-denial strategy, consulting a qualified immigration attorney is strongly recommended. An attorney can review the denial notice, assess the options, and advise on the best course of action specific to your case.
guide_steps.note: Do not treat this as optional. The stakes of an I-130 denial are high, and the correct path forward requires professional evaluation.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Evaluate and act on the appropriate option
guide_steps.text: Based on the denial reasons and legal advice, determine whether an appeal (Form EOIR-29 to the BIA), a motion to reopen, a motion to reconsider, or another strategy is appropriate. Act within the applicable deadlines.
guide_steps.note: Rahvana can guide you through general information about each option, but the final decision on which path to take should be made with qualified legal assistance.

citations.text: Form EOIR-29 — Notice of Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals

steps.step_short_description: General notice guidance · Biometrics, interview, or appointment
steps.step_description: USCIS may send notices that are not standard evidence requests — such as appointment notices (Form I-797C), interview notices, transfer notices, or fee adjustment requests. Follow these universal steps to respond appropriately.

guide_data.title: Respond to Other USCIS Notice or Request
guide_data.subtitle: USCIS issues various types of notices during petition processing. Identify your specific notice type, follow the required instructions, and ensure timely compliance.

alert.heading: Identify the Form Number and Heading
alert.body: Official USCIS notices are usually issued on Form I-797C (Notice of Action) or Form I-797. Look at the top-right header and notice type line to understand whether action is required or if it is purely informational.

common_rfe_reasons.title: Common notice types you may receive
common_rfe_reasons.subtitle: USCIS sends several standard communication types. Find your notice type below:

categories.label: Biometrics / ASC Appointment Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: USCIS schedules an appointment at an Application Support Center (ASC) to capture fingerprints, photo, and signature. This is common if biometric verification is needed.
evidence_examples: Bring the original appointment notice with barcode.
Bring government-issued photo ID (valid passport, driver's license).
If you cannot attend, follow the reschedule instructions on the notice immediately before the appointment date.
categories.important_note: Failing to appear for a biometrics appointment without rescheduling can result in petition abandonment and denial.

categories.label: Interview Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: While most consular I-130 petitions are decided without an in-person USCIS interview, USCIS occasionally requests a domestic petitioner interview or parent interview.
evidence_examples: Original civil documents (petitioner birth certificate, parent marriage certificate).
Proof of ongoing parent-child relationship (photos over time, travel records, communication).
Valid government-issued photo identification.
categories.important_note: Carefully review the checklist of items to bring on the interview notice and arrive 15 minutes before the scheduled time.

categories.label: Service Center Transfer Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: USCIS frequently transfers cases between service centers (e.g., Nebraska, Texas, Potomac, California, Vermont) to balance processing workloads across the agency.
evidence_examples: No action is required on your part.
Your receipt number remains unchanged.
Future correspondence will come from the new service center.
categories.important_note: A case transfer does not mean anything is wrong with your petition. It is routine workload management by USCIS.

categories.label: Fee Correction / Rejection Notice
categories.description: If payment could not be processed or an essential document was missing at intake, USCIS issues a notice explaining the intake issue.
evidence_examples: Check the specific rejection reason printed on the notice.
Submit corrected fee payment or missing signature promptly.
Ensure payment instrument (check, credit card authorization Form G-1450) is valid and funded.
categories.important_note: Pay close attention to any refiling instructions and deadline dates provided on the notice.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Read the entire notice thoroughly
guide_steps.text: Check the notice type in the header, read all instructions, and verify whether USCIS requires a response, an appearance, or if the notice is purely informational.
guide_steps.note: Look for specific keywords such as 'Action Required', 'Notice of Action', or 'Appointment Scheduled'.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check your USCIS online account
guide_steps.text: Log in to my.uscis.gov and check the 'Documents' tab for an electronic PDF copy of the notice. Online notices are often available days before physical mail arrives.
guide_steps.note: Ensure your mailing address in your USCIS account is completely accurate and up to date.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Note any deadlines or appointment dates
guide_steps.text: If the notice specifies an appointment date, time, and location, or gives a deadline to submit documents, mark it on your calendar immediately.
guide_steps.note: Never wait until the last week. If rescheduling is needed, USCIS generally requires requests to be submitted well ahead of the appointment date.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Comply with the exact instructions and retain proof
guide_steps.text: Attend the appointment or submit the requested documentation according to the exact mailing or online upload instructions. Keep copies of everything submitted, along with delivery tracking numbers or stamped appointment notices.
guide_steps.note: Save your stamped biometrics confirmation sheet or mailing receipt in your immigration records binder.
