doc_citizenship.title: Proof of U.S. Citizenship
doc_citizenship.sub: Establishes the petitioner's right to file for an IR-1 spouse

sections.title: What this is
sections.htmlContent: The petitioner, the U.S. citizen spouse, must prove their citizenship to USCIS when filing Form I-130. This is the foundational document of the entire petition.

sections.title: Accepted documents
sections.htmlContent:
USCIS accepts one of the following as proof of U.S. citizenship:

  • U.S. passport, valid or recently expired; most commonly used
  • U.S. birth certificate, issued by a U.S. state or county vital records office
  • Certificate of Naturalization (Form N-550), issued by USCIS after oath ceremony
  • Certificate of Citizenship (Form N-560), for those who acquired or derived citizenship through a parent
  • Consular Report of Birth Abroad (Form FS-240 / DS-1350), for those born abroad to a U.S. citizen parent

You do not need to submit originals for most of these, legible photocopies are typically accepted with Form I-130. Check the current I-130 instructions before filing.

sections.title: Name discrepancy
sections.htmlContent:
If the name on the citizenship document does not match the name used in the petition (e.g. due to marriage or legal name change), include legal proof of the name change:

  • Court order for name change
  • Marriage certificate showing the name change

sections.title: Key pitfall
sections.htmlContent: Avoid this: Do not submit an expired U.S. passport without also providing another valid proof. An expired passport alone may not be accepted, check the current I-130 filing instructions.

doc_relationship.title: Relationship Evidence
doc_relationship.sub: Proof the marriage is genuine and entered in good faith

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.htmlContent: USCIS adjudicators will assess whether the marriage is bona fide, entered in good faith for a genuine life together, not primarily to obtain immigration benefits. Evidence across multiple categories significantly strengthens the case.

sections.title: Strong evidence categories
sections.htmlContent:
Gather evidence across as many of these categories as possible:

  • Communication history, WhatsApp/call logs, screenshots of messages over time, email correspondence showing an ongoing relationship
  • Photos together, wedding photos, casual photos, photos across different dates and locations, family gatherings
  • Travel history, plane tickets, boarding passes, hotel bookings showing in-person visits
  • Shared finances, joint bank account statements, shared bills, financial transfers between spouses
  • Shared residence, lease agreements, utility bills, or mail showing a shared address
  • Family evidence, children together, family photos that show integration into each other's families
  • Affidavits, signed statements from family members or friends who personally know the couple and can attest to the relationship

sections.title: For the I-130 stage specifically
sections.htmlContent:
At the USCIS I-130 filing stage, the petitioner submits the I-130 along with supporting evidence. A strong bona fide marriage package typically includes:

  • At least 3–5 photos showing the couple together across different occasions
  • Evidence of ongoing communication (call logs or chat screenshots with metadata)
  • Evidence of at least one in-person visit (travel documentation)
  • Affidavits if direct joint evidence is limited

There is no single "required" evidence list from USCIS, the goal is to present a convincing overall picture of a genuine relationship. More varied evidence across categories is better than one large category alone.

sections.title: What to avoid
sections.htmlContent:
• Do not submit hundreds of pages of chat history, curate and organize
  • Avoid submitting only one type of evidence (e.g. photos only)
  • Ensure affidavits are signed, dated, and specific about how the writer knows the couple
  • Do not use generic template affidavits, they are easily spotted and carry little weight

doc_prior_marriage.title: Prior Marriage Termination Proof
doc_prior_marriage.sub: Required if either spouse had a previous marriage

sections.title: When this applies
sections.htmlContent:
This document is required if either the petitioner or the beneficiary was previously married. USCIS must confirm that every prior marriage ended legally before the current marriage began.

If neither spouse has a prior marriage, this item does not apply to your case.

sections.title: Accepted termination documents
sections.htmlContent:
• Divorce decree or divorce certificate, final court order ending the prior marriage
  • Annulment order, court order declaring the marriage void
  • Death certificate, if the prior spouse is deceased

sections.title: Pakistan-specific, divorce
sections.htmlContent:
In Pakistan, divorce proceedings vary by religious law. For Muslims, the process typically involves:

  • Talaq, the husband's pronouncement, registered with the Union Council, followed by a mandatory 90-day reconciliation period (iddat); Union Council issues a divorce certificate after this period
  • Khula, wife-initiated dissolution through Family Court; court issues the final decree
  • Judicial divorce, through Family Court; court issues the final decree

Important: For talaq, the divorce is not legally effective in Pakistan until the 90-day reconciliation period expires and the Union Council issues the divorce certificate. Ensure you have the final certificate, not just the initial notice.

sections.title: Translation requirement
sections.htmlContent: All divorce decrees and termination documents in Urdu or other non-English languages must be accompanied by a full certified English translation.

doc_translations.title: Translations
doc_translations.sub: Certified English translations of non-English documents

sections.title: USCIS translation requirement
sections.htmlContent: USCIS requires that every document not in English be accompanied by a full certified English translation. This applies to all stages, I-130, NVC, and consular.

sections.title: What "certified translation" means
sections.htmlContent:
USCIS defines a certified translation as one accompanied by a signed statement from the translator certifying:

  • They are competent to translate from the source language to English
  • The translation is accurate and complete to the best of their ability

The translator does not need to be a licensed professional or a notary, but they must not be the applicant or petitioner themselves.

sections.title: Documents that need translation
sections.htmlContent:
• Nikah Nama, typically in Urdu; full translation required
  • NADRA MRC, bilingual, but full translation of the Urdu portions is recommended to avoid questions
  • Birth certificate, if issued in Urdu or regional language
  • Divorce decree, if in Urdu or Sindhi etc.
  • Any other civil documents submitted to USCIS or the NVC

sections.title: Practical tips
sections.htmlContent:
• Use a translation service that issues a formal certification letter on their letterhead, it is more persuasive than a plain self-attestation
  • Keep the translated document together with the original, submit them as a pair
  • Do not translate only part of a document, the entire document must be translated

doc_passport_photos.title: Passport Photos
doc_passport_photos.sub: Required at consular and visa application stages

sections.title: When these are needed
sections.htmlContent:
Passport photos are not required for the USCIS I-130 petition filing. They are required at later stages:

  • The DS-260 immigrant visa application (online form submitted to the NVC)
  • At the consular interview, the U.S. Embassy in Islamabad typically requires passport-size photos

Gather them closer to those stages rather than now.

sections.title: U.S. visa photo specifications
sections.htmlContent:
• 2 × 2 inches (51 × 51 mm)
  • White or off-white plain background
  • Taken within the last 6 months
  • Full front view, neutral expression, eyes open
  • No glasses (as of 2016 U.S. visa photo rules)
  • Head coverings only for religious reasons, and must not obscure the face

The DS-260 online application accepts a digital photo upload, check the U.S. State Department's photo upload tool and specifications at the time of filing.

doc_parent_identity_match.title: Parent Identity & Name-Match Evidence
doc_parent_identity_match.sub: Resolving spelling and name variations for parent beneficiaries

sections.title: What this is
sections.htmlContent: USCIS needs to be certain that the parent you're sponsoring is the exact same person named on your birth certificate. Name mismatches across civil documents are common in many countries, especially where naming conventions, honorifics, or transliteration differ from Western formats. In Pakistan, for example, names are frequently written in a different order, or with a title added or dropped.

sections.title: Common types of discrepancies
sections.htmlContent:
• A different name order (first/last swapped)
  • A title or honorific added or dropped
  • A different spelling from transliteration
  • One document using a father's name, another using a spouse's name

sections.title: Official Correction
sections.htmlContent: If the discrepancy is significant, it's usually best to correct it at the source through your country's civil registry, in Pakistan, this means going to a NADRA office to correct your parent's CNIC/NICOP, using older records like school certificates as proof of the relationship, and then requesting a fresh Family Registration Certificate (FRC) with the correct name.

sections.title: One-and-the-Same Affidavits
sections.htmlContent: For minor spelling differences, most countries accept a sworn affidavit confirming both spellings refer to the same person, instead of a formal correction. In Pakistan, this needs to be signed by a close relative or family friend who knows your family well, and notarized by a registered Notary Public. Requirements can vary by province, so confirm the current process locally before preparing it.

doc_father_bona_fide_relationship.title: Bona Fide Father-Child Relationship Evidence
doc_father_bona_fide_relationship.sub: Proving financial and emotional ties if parents were unmarried at birth

sections.title: When this is required
sections.htmlContent: If you're sponsoring your biological father and your parents weren't legally married when you were born, you'll need to show a genuine father-child relationship existed before you turned 21, regardless of which country you're filing from.

sections.title: Financial support proof
sections.htmlContent:
• Remittances: Money transfer receipts showing your father sending money to you or your mother over the years
  • School fees: Admission sheets, school tuition receipts, or report cards bearing the father's signature or name as guardian.
  • Medical bills: Hospital registration sheets, vaccination cards, or prescription records mentioning the father's name as the responsible parent.

sections.title: Social & Emotional proof
sections.htmlContent:
• Photographs: Family photographs spanning different ages of the child, showing the father together with the child at birthdays, Eid, school events, or trips.
  • Letters/Messages: Old letters, emails, or chat logs showing communication between father and child.
  • Affidavits: Notarized sworn statements from school teachers, neighbors, or relatives who witnessed the father actively raising and supporting the child.

sections.title: DNA testing
sections.htmlContent: In cases where document proof is weak or questioned, USCIS or the Embassy may suggest DNA testing. Do not obtain DNA testing proactively on your own; wait for an official instruction from the Embassy or USCIS, as they require testing to be conducted through an AABB-accredited lab and follow a strict chain-of-custody protocol.

doc_stepparent_prior_marriages.title: Termination of Prior Marriages for Step-Relationship
doc_stepparent_prior_marriages.sub: Proving the step-relationship marriage is legally valid

sections.title: What is required
sections.htmlContent: For step-relationship petitions, you'll need to show that any earlier marriages of both your biological parent and your stepparent were legally ended before their current marriage. The step-relationship itself must have started before you turned 18. How this is proven depends on which country and legal system the marriage falls under.

sections.title: Talaq (Divorce)
sections.htmlContent: Divorce under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 requires a Divorce Certificate issued by the local Union Council, Cantonment Board, or Municipal Committee. This certificate only comes after a required 90-day notice and arbitration period, so a notice of Talaq alone, or a raw Talaqnama, isn't accepted as proof of legal termination.

sections.title: Khula / Judicial Dissolution
sections.htmlContent: If the wife initiated the divorce through Family Court (Khula), you'll need the certified Court Decree along with confirmation that the Union Council registered the decree and the waiting period was completed.

sections.title: If a different personal law applies
sections.htmlContent: Some marriages fall under a different law entirely, for example, the Christian Divorce Act, 1869 or the Hindu Marriage Act, 2017. In these cases, the divorce is generally granted directly by a Family Court after a case is filed, and it's usually not registered with a Union Council the way a Talaq or Khula is. What you'll need here is the Family Court decree itself, since a Union Council certificate typically won't exist.

sections.title: Death Certificates
sections.htmlContent: If a prior marriage ended in death, provide the civil death certificate from the relevant civil authority. Hospital or cemetery records alone generally aren't sufficient proof, regardless of country.

doc_adoption_decree.title: Final Adoption Decree
doc_adoption_decree.sub: Legal requirements for adoptive parent petitions

sections.title: U.S. Immigration Adoption Rules
sections.htmlContent: To qualify as an adoptive parent, the adoption must have taken place before you turned 16 (or 18 if adopting a biological sibling), and your adoptive parent must have had legal custody of you and lived with you for at least two years.

sections.title: When a country doesn't have a legal adoption system
sections.htmlContent:
Some countries don't have adoption as a legal category at all, instead they use a guardianship or custody arrangement that doesn't fully end the biological parents' rights or make the child a legal heir. U.S. immigration law requires a full, final adoption decree that does both of those things, so a guardianship order from one of these countries, no matter how it's worded, can't be submitted as a final adoption decree.

Pakistan is a common example: Pakistani courts can only issue a guardianship order under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, and this doesn't end a biological parent's legal rights or make the child a legal heir.

The orphan petition route (I-600): In these cases, the orphan petition process is generally the path available instead. To qualify, you generally need to meet the U.S. definition of an "orphan", for example, both parents have died, disappeared, or have irrevocably released the child in writing for emigration and adoption. From there, the adoption can happen abroad (with Form I-600 filed) or after arriving in the U.S.

sections.title: How to comply
sections.htmlContent: If your country has a genuine legal adoption process, an immigration attorney can confirm your decree meets U.S. federal adoption criteria. If it doesn't, as in Pakistan, your existing guardianship order isn't wasted; it can still support your case as evidence of who's been caring for you, even though it can't stand in as the adoption decree itself.

doc_adoption_custody_residence.title: Legal Custody & Joint Residence Evidence
doc_adoption_custody_residence.sub: Establishing the 2-year physical and legal custody requirement

sections.title: The Two-Year Rule
sections.htmlContent: You need to show your adoptive parent had legal custody of you and lived with you for at least two years before the petition is filed. These two years can happen before, during, or after the final adoption decree, and this requirement is the same regardless of which country you're filing from.

sections.title: Proof of Legal Custody
sections.htmlContent: Legal custody is established by a court order, decree, or official government document. Informal custody arrangements or verbal agreements do not count toward the two-year legal custody requirement.

sections.title: Proof of Joint Residence
sections.htmlContent:
Provide documents showing a shared household over the two-year period:

  • School enrollment records listing the parent's address and name as guardian
  • Immunization or hospital files showing shared address
  • Rental deeds or utility invoices naming both parties at the same property
  • Government census records or local police registration certificates

doc_name_change.title: Name Change or Identity Discrepancy Evidence
doc_name_change.sub: Resolving spelling and profile mismatches across records

sections.title: Handling Name Mismatches
sections.htmlContent: Mismatches across your birth certificate, national ID, school records, or passport can trigger delays or Requests for Evidence in any country, so it's worth sorting these out before you file.

sections.title: Civil Registry Correction
sections.htmlContent: To correct a name or date of birth, visit your country's civil registry office with supporting documents like matriculation certificates, older passports, or court decrees. In Pakistan, this means a NADRA office, which will issue a revised CNIC/NICOP and FRC. Note that NADRA generally only corrects English-spelling mistakes through this process, a full name change requires the separate procedure below.

sections.title: Gazette Notification & Deed Poll
sections.htmlContent: For a full legal name change in Pakistan, you'll need a notarized affidavit, a published notice in local newspapers, and registration with the official Gazette of Pakistan. The published Gazette notice is what carries real legal weight, it's what banks, passport offices, and other institutions will actually ask to see.

sections.title: Sworn Affidavits
sections.htmlContent: If your records genuinely can't be corrected, a notarized affidavit from close relatives explaining the mismatch can serve as backup evidence in most jurisdictions.

doc_secondary_relationship.title: Secondary Parent-Child Relationship Evidence
doc_secondary_relationship.sub: Alternative evidence when a primary birth record is unavailable

sections.title: When to use secondary evidence
sections.htmlContent: If a primary birth certificate is unavailable (e.g. not registered at birth or destroyed), secondary evidence must be submitted alongside a Non-Availability Certificate from the local authority.

sections.title: Matriculation and School Certificates
sections.htmlContent: Official school board certificates that list both parents' names are considered strong secondary evidence by USCIS. In Pakistan, this typically means Matriculation or Intermediate certificates from the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE).

sections.title: Civil and Family Certificates
sections.htmlContent: NGovernment-issued family registration documents showing your parent-child relationship are accepted as supporting evidence, in Pakistan, this includes NADRA Family Registration Certificates (FRC) or B-Forms.

sections.title: Religious and Local Records
sections.htmlContent: Nikah Namas (for parents), baptism certificates, or birth entries in local hospital registers listing parent names are also helpful secondary sources.

doc_record_unavailability.title: Record Unavailability Evidence
doc_record_unavailability.sub: How to prove a civil document genuinely cannot be obtained

sections.title: What is a Non-Availability Certificate (NAC)
sections.htmlContent: If you can't get a primary birth or marriage certificate, you'll need a certificate confirming no record exists, issued by the relevant local civil authority. In Pakistan, this is issued by the Union Council, Municipal Committee, Cantonment Board, or Metropolitan Corporation.

sections.title: Key elements of a valid NAC
sections.htmlContent:
To be accepted by USCIS/Embassy, the NAC must:

  • Be issued on the official letterhead of the local authority
  • Explicitly state the name of the child/person, date of birth, place of birth, and parents' names
  • State that the register for that year was searched and no record was found
  • Be signed and stamped by the Secretary of the Union Council or the designated registrar

sections.title: Important rule
sections.htmlContent: This certificate alone isn't enough anywhere, always pair it with other secondary evidence, like school certificates, old family registration documents, or an affidavit. Some office-level specifics can differ, so it's worth confirming directly with your local authority when you apply.

sections.title: Why this is needed
sections.htmlContent: At the NVC and consular stages, your parent needs to document their full marriage history, proving their marriage to your other parent (if applicable) and proving any earlier marriages were legally ended. Required documents vary by country and by the specific law that governed the marriage.

sections.title: Required documents
sections.htmlContent:
• Nikah Nama: The traditional Islamic marriage contract. It Must be fully translated and certified.
  • NADRA Marriage Registration Certificate (MRC): The official bilingual certificate issued by the local Union Council/NADRA registrar. Highly recommended to submit both the Nikah Nama and the MRC to avoid RFEs.
  • Divorce Certificates: Union Council-issued final divorce certificates or court decrees.
  • Death Certificates: Union Council/NADRA-issued death certificates for former spouses.

birth-cert-hh.title: Birth Certificate, Household Member
birth-cert-hh.intro: Proves the parent–child relationship between the household member and the petitioner.

sections.title: What this is
sections.body: The official birth certificate of the household member (the child). For Pakistan cases, this is ideally the NADRA Computerized Birth Registration Certificate (CBRC).

sections.title: Why it is needed
sections.body: When a child's income is being combined with the petitioner's through Form I-864A, the parent-child relationship must be established. The birth certificate naming the petitioner as a parent does this.

sections.title: Translation
sections.body: If in Urdu, a certified English translation must accompany the original.

sections.title: Watch out for
sections.body: Ensure the name on the birth certificate matches the name used in CEAC and on other filed documents. Discrepancies should be addressed proactively.

birth-cert-sponsor.title: Birth Certificate of Petitioner / Sponsor
birth-cert-sponsor.intro: Used when the household member is a parent or sibling of the petitioner, to show the shared family link.

sections.title: What this is
sections.body: The petitioner's own birth certificate. In a parent or sibling household-member scenario, this document helps establish the family relationship between the petitioner and the household member.

sections.title: For parent relationship
sections.body: Shows that the household member (parent) is listed on the petitioner's birth certificate, establishing the parent-child link.

sections.title: For sibling relationship
sections.body: The petitioner's birth certificate, combined with the household member's birth certificate, can show shared parentage when both list the same parents.

marriage-cert-hh.title: Marriage Certificate, Household Member
marriage-cert-hh.intro: Establishes the spousal relationship between the household member and the petitioner.

sections.title: What this is
sections.body: The civil marriage certificate proving that the household member is legally married to the petitioner. For Pakistan cases, this is the Nikah Nama and/or NADRA MRC.

sections.title: Why it is needed
sections.body: When the petitioner's spouse is acting as a household member contributing income through Form I-864A, the marriage must be documented to support that household connection.

sections.title: Translation
sections.body: The Nikah Nama (in Urdu) requires a full certified English translation.

shared-residence.title: Proof of Shared Residence
shared-residence.intro: Demonstrates that the household member and the petitioner share the same household address.

sections.title: What this is
sections.body: Documents showing a shared residential address between the petitioner and the household member. This reinforces the household income contribution basis.

sections.title: Accepted examples
sections.body:
• Lease agreement naming both parties
  • Utility bills addressed to the same household
  • Bank statements or tax returns showing the same address
  • Official correspondence addressed to both at the same address

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.body: The household member concept in I-864A depends on a genuine shared household. Residence proof strengthens the basis for including their income.

id-doc-hh.title: Identity Document, Household Member
id-doc-hh.intro: Confirms the identity of the household member named in the I-864A.

sections.title: What to provide
sections.body: A government-issued identity document for the household member. For Pakistan cases, this is typically the CNIC (Computerized National Identity Card) or a passport biographic page.

sections.title: Consistency
sections.body: The name on the identity document must match exactly the name used in CEAC and on the I-864A form. Any discrepancy should be explained or corrected.

family-link.title: Supporting Family-Link Evidence
family-link.intro: Used when the household member's relationship is more distant or non-standard, to establish the household connection.

sections.title: When this applies
sections.body: For household members who are other relatives (aunt, uncle, cousin, non-relative household member), standard civil records like birth certificates may not directly show the link. Additional supporting evidence helps.

sections.title: What to include
sections.body:
• Family tree documentation or affidavit of relationship
  • Any relevant civil records showing the family connection
  • Shared address or financial co-dependence records

sections.title: Note
sections.body: For non-standard relationships, consulting an immigration attorney before relying on household member income is strongly recommended.
